context-aware-evaluation.takeaway: Adding document context to a translation metric only at inference trades sentence-level accuracy for system-level gains. Cont-COMET trains COMET with selected context, as human annotators see it, and largely removes that trade-off.
context-aware-evaluation.question: Human annotators judge translations within documents, while many automatic metrics score isolated sentences. How can a metric use context without introducing noise or weakening sentence-level judgments?

method.title: Select relevant context
method.text: Rank surrounding reference sentences by semantic similarity and distance, keeping the most relevant context within the encoder’s input limit.

method.title: Encode the target sentence
method.text: Combine preceding and following context with the source, reference, and translation; pool representations over the target sentence.

method.title: Train with context
method.text: Fine-tune COMET using contextualized examples and human ratings, matching the information available during human annotation.

context-aware-evaluation.prior_work: Neural metrics such as COMET (Rei et al., 2020) score each sentence from its source, reference, and hypothesis, although WMT human annotation has included document context since 2019. Vernikos et al. (2022) encoded preceding sentences when computing scores and concluded that two preceding sentences work best; the paper argues that this conclusion was not tested thoroughly and notes the approach's poor segment-level correlation. Cont-COMET uses both preceding and following context, selects it by relevance, and trains the metric with it.

contextual-asr.takeaway: A transcript can contain clues to its own recognition errors. Retrieving context from the document and related documents helps a correction model use those clues.
contextual-asr.question: Sentence-level correction misses information elsewhere in a transcript. Simply adding surrounding sentences can introduce noise; how can an ASR correction model retrieve the context it needs?

method.title: Build a context datastore
method.text: Store contextual representations from the current document or the wider dataset, allowing correction to access information beyond its immediate sentence.

method.title: Retrieve through attention
method.text: Add a kNN attention layer to a BART correction model, combining retrieved context with local representations.

method.title: Support two timing modes
method.text: Online correction builds the datastore incrementally; offline correction also accesses following context using the online datastore as initialization.

findings.label: AISHELL-1 CER, online mode

metadata_override.abstract: Contextual information, including the sentences in the same document and in other documents of the dataset, plays a crucial role in improving the accuracy of document-level ASR Error Correction (AEC), while most previous works ignore this. In this paper, we propose a context-aware method that utilizes a k-Nearest Neighbors ( kNN) approach to enhance the AEC model by retrieving a datastore containing contextual information. We conduct experiments on two English and two Chinese datasets, and the results demonstrate that our proposed model can effectively utilize contextual information to improve document-level AEC. Furthermore, the context information from the whole dataset provides even better results.

contextual-asr.prior_work: Most ASR error correction (AEC) models, such as BART-based correctors (Zhao et al., 2021), work one sentence at a time. Document-level MT offers two ways to add context: a separate context encoder (sent2sent), which Wang et al. (2021, 2022b) applied to ASR correction, and multi-sentence input (doc2doc). The paper argues that both widen attention, which limits context length and adds unselected noise. kNN-MT (Khandelwal et al., 2020b) instead retrieves decoder states from a datastore built on training data; this work retrieves attention keys and values from the current document or test set.

dsgram.takeaway: Good grammatical correction must preserve meaning, avoid unnecessary edits, and read fluently. DSGram scores these dimensions separately and adapts their importance to each sentence.
dsgram.question: LLMs often produce valid corrections that differ from a gold reference, or rewrite more than necessary. How should evaluation balance meaning, editing restraint, and fluency?

method.title: Score three dimensions
method.text: Use an LLM to assess semantic coherence, edit level, and fluency directly from the original and corrected sentences.

method.title: Adapt the weights
method.text: Generate pairwise criterion comparisons, check their consistency with the Analytic Hierarchy Process, and derive sentence-specific weights.

method.title: Combine and validate
method.text: Aggregate the weighted scores and compare against human judgments; use GPT-4 annotations to fine-tune smaller evaluators.

dsgram.prior_work: Reference-based GEC metrics such as M², ERRANT, and BLEU depend on gold corrections that may not cover every valid edit, and they miss the over-correction typical of LLM correctors (Fang et al. 2023). Reference-free metrics follow Asano et al. (2017): SOME scores grammaticality, fluency, and meaning preservation with three BERT models and combines them by a weighted sum. DSGram merges the largely redundant grammaticality and fluency scores, adds an Edit Level criterion for over-correction, and replaces the single weighting with sentence-specific weights that an LLM derives through AHP; IMPARA appears as a further reference-free baseline in Table 3.

eama.takeaway: News captions need names and events that an image alone cannot reveal. EAMA teaches a multimodal LLM, InstructBLIP, to find the relevant sentences and entities in the article before writing the caption.
eama.question: A news photograph shows a scene, but its article supplies names and events. How can a model select the right entity information without overwhelming caption generation with the full article?

method.text: Train on entity-aware sentence selection and entity selection alongside news image captioning, using supervision derived from existing caption data.

method.title: Extract relevant information

method.title: Generate with selected context

metadata_override.abstract: News image captioning requires model to generate an informative caption rich in entities, with the news image and the associated news article. Current MLLMs still bear limitations in handling entity information in news image captioning tasks. Besides, generating high-quality news image captions requires a trade-off between sufficiency and conciseness of textual input information. To explore the potential of MLLMs and address problems we discovered, we propose EAMA : an Entity-Aware Multimodal Alignment based approach for News Image Captioning. Our approach first aligns the MLLM with two extra alignment tasks: Entity-Aware Sentence Selection task and Entity Selection task, together with News Image Captioning task. The aligned MLLM will utilize the additional entity-related information extracted by itself to supplement the textual input while generating news image captions. Our approach achieves better results than all previous models on two mainstream news image captioning datasets.

error-robust-retrieval.takeaway: A misspelled character is a poor retrieval query. RERIC combines pronunciation, shape, and surrounding context to find useful training examples without retraining the correction model.
error-robust-retrieval.question: A spelling-correction system may miss an error even when similar examples exist in its training data. How can retrieval remain useful when the query itself contains an incorrect character?

method.title: Represent errors robustly
method.text: Build retrieval keys from a character’s phonetic and morphological features plus surrounding context, reducing dependence on its potentially incorrect meaning.

method.title: Retrieve and rerank
method.text: Retrieve nearest neighbors from training data, then rerank them using overlap between their surrounding n-grams and the input.

method.title: Combine correction probabilities
method.text: Interpolate the retrieval distribution with the base model’s predictions to choose corrected characters, without additional model training.

metadata_override.abstract: Chinese Spelling Check (CSC) aims to detect and correct error tokens in Chinese contexts, which has a wide range of applications. However, it is confronted with the challenges of insufficient annotated data and the issue that previous methods may actually not fully leverage the existing datasets. In this paper, we introduce our plug-and-play retrieval method with error-robust information for Chinese Spelling Check (RERIC), which can be directly applied to existing CSC models. The datastore for retrieval is built completely based on the training data, with elaborate designs according to the characteristics of CSC. Specifically, we employ multimodal representations that fuse phonetic, morphologic, and contextual information in the calculation of query and key during retrieval to enhance robustness against potential errors. Furthermore, in order to better judge the retrieved candidates, the n-gram surrounding the token to be checked is regarded as the value and utilized for specific reranking. The experiment results on the SIGHAN benchmarks demonstrate that our proposed method achieves substantial improvements over existing work.

error-robust-retrieval.prior_work: Multimodal Chinese Spelling Check (CSC) models such as SpellGCN, PLOME, and REALISE build phonetic and glyph information into the corrector during training. Retrieval methods such as kNN-LM and kNN-MT (Khandelwal et al., 2019, 2020) instead attach a datastore of training examples to a trained model and interpolate its predictions at inference. RERIC, which the authors describe as the first retrieval-augmented CSC method, adapts that pattern to queries that may contain the error: keys combine pronunciation, glyph shape, and distance-weighted context, and candidates are reranked by 3-gram overlap.

nlg-evaluation-survey.takeaway: LLMs can evaluate generated text in several distinct ways. This survey organizes the methods and explains the reliability, cost, and control trade-offs behind each choice.
nlg-evaluation-survey.question: LLM-based evaluation ranges from probability scores to prompted judges and specialized models. Which design choices distinguish these approaches, and what must be checked before relying on their judgments?

method.text: Group the literature into LLM-derived metrics, prompting, fine-tuning, and human–LLM collaborative evaluation.

method.title: Compare evaluation designs
method.text: Examine scoring, pairwise comparison, ranking, Boolean questions, and error analysis, alongside training data and evaluator outputs.

method.title: Identify unresolved problems
method.text: Analyze reliability, robustness, bias, interpretability, and how human participation can support evaluation quality.

nlg-evaluation-survey.scope: The survey covers about 100 works found through June 2024, limited to LLMs with more than one billion parameters on tasks whose input and output are natural language. It excludes evaluation of LLM capabilities, NLG datasets and benchmarks, and statistical analysis of metrics.

metadata_override.abstract: Evaluating natural language generation (NLG) is a vital but challenging problem in natural language processing. Traditional evaluation metrics mainly capturing content (e.g., n-gram) overlap between system outputs and references are far from satisfactory, and large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT have demonstrated great potential in NLG evaluation in recent years. Various automatic evaluation methods based on LLMs have been proposed, including metrics derived from LLMs, prompting LLMs, fine-tuning LLMs, and human–LLM collaborative evaluation. In this survey, we first give a taxonomy of LLM-based NLG evaluation methods, and discuss their pros and cons, respectively. Lastly, we discuss several open problems in this area and point out future research directions.

glance.prior: Earlier surveys cover automatic metrics or human evaluation practice (Celikyilmaz, Clark, and Gao 2020; Gehrmann, Clark, and Sellam 2023); this survey covers LLM-based NLG evaluation, not evaluation of LLMs' abilities.
glance.limitation: Coverage ends in June 2024, and the cross-paradigm performance comparison rests on one summarization benchmark, SummEval, because fine-tuned evaluators were tested under incomparable settings.

nlg-evaluation-survey.prior_work: Earlier surveys review automatic NLG metrics or human evaluation practice (Celikyilmaz, Clark, and Gao 2020; Sai, Mohankumar, and Khapra 2023; Gehrmann, Clark, and Sellam 2023), and the authors note that none addresses LLM-based evaluation. Surveys on evaluating LLMs' capabilities (Zhuang et al. 2023; Chang et al. 2024) answer a different question and are excluded. This survey instead organizes about 100 works that use LLMs as evaluators into four paradigms and compares them on flexibility, reproducibility, performance, and cost.

seq2seq-data2text.takeaway: A high generation score does not explain what a model gets wrong. Fine-grained human annotation reveals how copying, pre-training, and dataset structure affect data-to-text errors.
seq2seq-data2text.question: Seq2Seq systems can produce fluent descriptions that omit or misstate their input data. Which model choices reduce these errors, and which weaknesses disappear inside aggregate evaluation scores?

method.title: Compare representative models
method.text: Evaluate Transformer, a pointer-generator Transformer, T5-small, T5-base, and BART-base on E2E, WebNLG, WikiBio, and ToTTo.

method.title: Annotate specific errors
method.text: Use an adapted MQM framework with eight error types covering accuracy and fluency, rather than relying only on automatic scores.

method.title: Analyze the contributing factors

metadata_override.abstract: With the rapid development of deep learning, Seq2Seq paradigm has become prevalent for end-to-end data-to-text generation, and the BLEU scores have been increasing in recent years. However, it is widely recognized that there is still a gap between the quality of the texts generated by models and the texts written by human. In order to better understand the ability of Seq2Seq models, evaluate their performance and analyze the results, we choose to use Multidimensional Quality Metric(MQM) to evaluate several representative Seq2Seq models on end-to-end data-to-text generation. We annotate the outputs of five models on four datasets with eight error types and find that 1) copy mechanism is helpful for the improvement in Omission and Inaccuracy Extrinsic errors but it increases other types of errors such as Addition; 2) pre-training techniques are highly effective, and pre-training strategy and model size are very significant; 3) the structure of the dataset also influences the model’s performance greatly; 4) some specific types of errors are generally challenging for seq2seq models.

results_table.caption: Table 5 (ToTTo rows; the Positive-Negative Aspect column, 0 for every model on ToTTo, is omitted), with each model's overall ToTTo human score from Table 3. Error columns are severity-weighted, length-normalized error scores from human MQM annotation of 80 outputs per model, lower is better; the human score is 100 minus the summed error scores, up to rounding, higher is better. ptr-gen is the Transformer with a copy mechanism. On ToTTo, copying reduces Omission but raises Addition and Word Form; the rise in Addition also appears on WikiBio and WebNLG, but not on E2E.

glance.result: ToTTo human error scores: adding a copy mechanism to Transformer cuts Omission from 19.74 to 7.48 but raises Addition from 4.38 to 11.01 (lower is better).
glance.prior: Ferreira et al. (2019) compare pipeline and end-to-end data-to-text systems, and PolyTope (Huang et al., 2020) annotates summarization errors; this work applies MQM error annotation to five Seq2Seq models on four datasets.
glance.limitation: Each model–dataset score rests on 80 annotated outputs, and only models up to 220M parameters were tested; T5-large and BART-large were omitted for compute reasons.

seq2seq-data2text.prior_work: Ferreira et al. (2019) compared pipeline and end-to-end architectures for neural data-to-text generation, and Thomson and Reiter (2020) proposed a protocol for human evaluation of accuracy. Most model comparisons still rely on BLEU or ROUGE, which can disagree with human judgment (Novikova et al., 2017a; Reiter, 2018), and existing human evaluations cover few samples, datasets, models, or error dimensions. This study adapts the MQM-based PolyTope scheme of Huang et al. (2020), developed for summarization, to annotate five Seq2Seq models on four data-to-text datasets.

themis.takeaway: An evaluator should explain its scores and accept the criteria a task needs. Themis trains an open model to provide both, without requiring a reference answer.
themis.question: Reference answers are often unavailable, and fixed metrics cannot easily accommodate new criteria. Can a specialized language model deliver flexible ratings and explanations that align with human judgment?

metadata_override.abstract: The evaluation of natural language generation (NLG) tasks is a significant and longstanding research area. With the recent emergence of powerful large language models (LLMs), some studies have turned to LLM-based automatic evaluation methods, which demonstrate great potential to become a new evaluation paradigm following traditional string-based and model-based metrics. However, despite the improved performance of existing methods, they still possess some deficiencies, such as dependency on references and limited evaluation flexibility. Therefore, in this paper, we meticulously construct a large-scale NLG evaluation corpus NLG-Eval with annotations from both human and GPT-4 to alleviate the lack of relevant data in this field. Furthermore, we propose Themis, an LLM dedicated to NLG evaluation, which has been trained with our designed multi-perspective consistency verification and rating-oriented preference alignment methods. Themis can conduct flexible and interpretable evaluations without references, and it exhibits superior evaluation performance on various NLG tasks, simultaneously generalizing well to unseen tasks and surpassing other evaluation models, including GPT-4.

glance.prior: G-Eval prompts proprietary GPT models; Prometheus needs references, and Auto-J and TIGERScore lack customizable criteria. This work trains an open 8B evaluator that is reference-free, takes custom criteria, and explains ratings.
glance.limitation: Prompted GPT-4 still leads on dialogue-response (Topical-Chat) and translation (WMT23) evaluation, which the paper attributes to GPT-4's stronger dialogue and multilingual abilities.

themis.prior_work: Prompting approaches such as G-Eval ask proprietary LLMs such as GPT-4 to score, compare, or rank outputs; the paper notes that they are costly and can be irreproducible. Fine-tuned evaluators such as Prometheus, Auto-J, TIGERScore, and InstructScore train open models on human or GPT-4 judgments, but each either needs references or lacks customizable criteria (Table 1). Themis provides both properties with explanations, and adds consistency-based data selection and rating-guided preference alignment.
